newsitem.title: SURINAM: FEATURE-Suriname government confounds, confirms critics.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Suriname government confounds, confirms critics.

text.p: Can a leopard really change its spots?

That is the question in this former Dutch colony, where the new government, with its roots in the isolationist, free-spending military dictatorship of the 1980s, has both confirmed and confounded critics' fears during its first eight months in power, local businessmen and analysts say.

The leopard in question is Desi Bouterse, who led military coups that seized power in this South American country of 430,000 people in 1980 and 1990. A five-party coalition led by Bouterse's National Democratic Party (NDP) installed Jules Wijdenbosch as president last September, sparking fears that a fragile economic recovery was in the wrong hands.

Former President Ronald Venetiaan, elected in 1991 in Suriname's first democratic elections for more than a decade, employed tight fiscal and monetary policies to dramatic effect. A sliding Surinamese guilder was stabilised, inflation slashed from nearly 600 percent in 1994 to less than one percent in 1996 and economic contraction turned into steady growth rates of three to four percent per year.

Wijdenbosch, vice president and finance minister during Bouterse's military rule, was thought to be the last person to keep the reform programme on track. "When he was last in government the joke was that dollars were literally flying out of the Central Bank's windows," one local banker said.
FISCAL POLICY IS MAIN CONCERN

The new government has gone some way to reviving those fears, particularly with its fiscal policy. "Fiscal policy is a mess and that's a big concern. This country cannot afford to go back to high inflation again," one local businessman said.

Surinam, with its small population and huge potential in mining and forestry, was listed as the 17th richest country in the world in terms of natural and human resources in a recent World Bank report. But a costly guerrilla war in the late 1980s and lax controls on government spending saw the economy collapse. National per capita income dropped from more than $3,000 just after independence in 1975 to $1,300 now.

Wijdenbosch has shown himself to be prone to populist policies at key moments, analysts say. They point to a recent wage dispute in which workers at state logging company Bruynzeel who were holding out for a 50 percent pay increase were promised a 60 percent hike by Wijdenbosch, in spite of management's protests that it could afford only 10 percent.
The state sector remains grossly inflated. "There are 100,000 people on the state payroll but only half of them actually work. The rest just pick up their checks," the local banker said.
With a number of get-rich-quick savings schemes now on the point of collapse, analysts fear that the government may be tempted into a costly bailout.
SIGNS OF DISCPLINE

But there are positive signs too. A new 15 percent value added tax will come into effect in July, subsidies on electricity and water are to be eliminated and the floating currency regime has been maintained.

A recent report by Florida-based Hamilton Bank NA, which handled a $20 million Surinam bond placement in April, praised Wijdenbosch for continuing Venetiaan's reforms. "The government has defied some of the initial scepticism about its economic management by consolidating the macroeconomic achievements of the previous government," the report said.

The International Monetary Fund sees inflation rising slightly to 20 percent and growth remaining at four percent this year. Most encouraging, analysts say, is the government's apparent commitment to attracting foreign investment and privatising an array of about 180 state companies.

Canadian and U.S. gold companies are poised to start developing concessions granted under previous governments. After ruling out a controversial plan to sell massive tracts of Amazon rainforest to Asian logging companies the government is looking into a ground-breaking joint venture between Bruynzeel and a U.S. investment group for sustainable logging.

"This is a strong government, they make decisions. They might make some mistakes but that's okay," said Henk Ramdin, president of Aluminum Company of America's Suralco, which accounts for about 75 percent of Suriname's export earnings.
BOUTERSE IS MAN BEHIND THE SCENES

But the enigma behind the direction of Surinam remains Bouterse. Few doubt he is controlling government policy from behind the scenes. He flirted with alternative role models such as Libya and Cuba in the 1980s but many say he now recognises the inevitability of free market policies.

Wijdenbosch's election caused alarm in the Netherlands, home to about 250,000 Surinamese. The murder of 15 opposition activists in 1982 led to a cutoff in Dutch aid and an armed uprising that cost 500 lives and drove 15,000 people into exile. But many Surinamese feel Dutch concern over Bouterse's continued influence verges on paranoia.
"They're not objective. They will go a long way to criticise this government," one local businessman said.
Surinamese officials say they want a "businesslike" relationship with the Netherlands and insist that Bouterse's role in government policy should not be questioned.

"Everyone makes mistakes, but if people want him to make a comeback by voting for his party they (the Netherlands) have to accept that because that is democracy," National Assembly Speaker Indradevi Djwalapersad told Reuters.

Behind the dispute lies a growing probability that Bouterse will be tried in the Netherlands on charges of drug trafficking in the 1980s. Dutch Attorney General Docters van Leeuwen said in April that enough evidence had been gathered to proceed with the case against Bouterse within a year.
Two days later Wijdenbosch announced that Bouterse had been made Suriname's first state adviser with the role of advising the president on political and social matters.

In an interview with Dutch television in late May Bouterse acknowledged that his appointment was meant as a signal to The Hague and warned that he would have the last laugh. "When you're finished with your joke, it will be my turn," he said.
